https://www.swindonadvertiser.co.uk/news.text: Events Leisure People Swindon Scout off to 2027 World Scout Jamboree in Poland By Michael Ribbeck Reporter Share 0 Comments Eloise Cooper is representing UK (Image: Martyn Milner) This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. A Scout who describes the movement as her "place to belong" is set to take part in an international jamboree. Eloise Cooper, from Swindon, has been selected to represent the UK as a volunteer for the 2027 World Scout Jamboree. The event will take place in Gdansk, Poland, where she will join a team helping to organise and deliver the global gathering. Ms Cooper, who will be part of the International Service Team, will contribute to the smooth running of the jamboree by supporting outdoor activities, cultural events, and large-scale celebrations that highlight the diversity of global Scouting. She said: "Scouting has helped me develop confidence, resilience, and encouraged me to try new things. "Scouts has given me so many learning opportunities. Read more Family-owned demolition company collapses into administration after 23 years "I feel at home in Scouting, it is my place to belong. "This is my opportunity to give something back to young people and help deliver a fantastic event for young people from almost every nation on earth." Held every four years, the World Scout Jamboree brings together more than 50,000 Scouts from nearly every country for an international celebration of friendship, culture, and outdoor adventure. The 2027 edition, set against the backdrop of Poland’s history and traditions, is set to be a unique experience for all involved. Eloise is one of 600 UK volunteers who will help bring the jamboree to life. Chief Scout Dwayne Fields praised the UK team. He said: "Congratulations to Eloise and all the UK volunteers heading to the World Scout Jamboree in Poland. "Opportunities like this are what Scouting is all about, bringing people together, building confidence, and showing young people what’s possible when they step outside their comfort zone. "The Jamboree is more than an event, it’s a chance to connect with the world, to learn from different cultures, and to come back inspired to make a difference at home. "I’ve no doubt Eloise will grab this experience with both hands and make the most of every moment." https://www.digi24.ro/stiri/externe/mili.text: Un militar cu grad înalt din cadrul Armatei SUA a fost arestat în Marea Britanie sub suspiciunea că a ajutat serviciile de informaţii ruse, a anunţat poliţia britanică marţi, transmit Reuters şi AFP. Bărbatul în vârstă de 41 de ani a fost reţinut marţi în apropierea oraşului Gloucester, din vestul Angliei, şi se află în prezent în custodia poliţiei, la o secţie din Londra, a precizat poliţia. El a fost arestat sub suspiciunea comiterii unor infracţiuni prevăzute de secţiunile 1 şi 3 din Legea privind Securitatea Naţională (National Security Act), care vizează obţinerea sau divulgarea de informaţii protejate şi sprijinirea unui serviciu de informaţii străin. Poliţia a menţionat că ţara vizată de aceste acuzaţii este Rusia. Directorul FBI, Kash Patel, a declarat că „această importantă arestare vizează acuzaţii de spionaj, aspect care constituie un motiv de maximă îngrijorare pentru Statele Unite şi aliaţii noştri”. Generalul de brigadă Sean Stinchon, care conduce Comandamentului de contrainformaţii al Armatei SUA, a subliniat că „presupusul comportament al unui militar cu grad înalt, căruia i-au fost încredinţate informaţii sensibile, serveşte drept un semnal de alarmă că ameninţările interne sunt reale şi persistente”. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmx2.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Russia does not provide numbers of its fallen soldiers By Olga Ivshina Â and Â Yaroslava Kiryukhina ,Â BBC Russian Published 25 November 2026 At least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, according to Russian government statistics analysed by the BBC. The leaked Rosstat data reveal how the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has fundamentally changed mortality patterns in Russia, and show the high cost paid in human life in a war that Vladimir Putin had assumed would last only days but is now almost five years old. BBC Russian has had access to more than 11 million death records from 2021 to September 2026, after a hack by Belarusian group Cyber Partisans BY and Ukraine's Silent Crow. Russia's statistics agency admitted to a cyber-attack, but denied any protected information had been leaked. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Wednesday that only Russia's defence ministry could officially report data on losses: "I suggest no other data be taken into account." The defence ministry has not released any official casualty figures for several years. Together with independent Russian outlet Mediazona, BBC Russian has compared the Rosstat data with its own list of confirmed military deaths, pulled from open sources since the start of the invasion, and it has found matches for 90% of the records. Military experts estimate that the BBC's list of 290,012 deaths, gleaned from official reports, social media, new memorials and graves, may account for 45-55% of the true death toll, which would range from 527,295 to 644,471. The records show that 65% of 18 to 24 year-olds in Russia who lost their lives in 2025 died in the war. For those aged 25-34 the number was 59%. Only among 45 to 54 year-olds does cardiovascular disease claim more Russian lives than the conflict. The data also reveal the extent of losses in specific areas of Ukraine. Some 20,000 Russian soldiers died fighting for control of 10 Ukrainian villages whose combined pre-war population was 12,000. During the fight for one small village called Andriivka, south of the town of Bakhmut in Donetsk region, 1,122 Russians lost their lives. Before the war 74 people lived there. Russia does not give public figures for losses sustained since the war began in February 2022. And two years ago Rosstat stopped publishing data of deaths from external causes, which was used to gauge the extent of military losses. For example, only 70% of deaths we have established of soldiers from the occupied regions of Donetsk and Luhansk in eastern Ukraine who fought in the Russian army were accounted for in the Rosstat files. Overall, the Rosstat dataset confirms the trends that we have observed with our own count. Ukrainian losses were last put at about 50,000 by President Volodymyr Zelensky in July 2026, but another list based on open sources by the anonymous UA Losses website puts the figure at 115,952. How we came to a figure near half a million The Rosstat dataset contains no names but does include ages, places of residence, places of death and also circumstances of death. We have filtered the records first by location, leaving only Ukraine as well as Russian border regions that saw incursions by the Ukrainian army. Next, we identified 425,174 entries explicitly indicating a military-related cause of death, such as explosions or shrapnel during combat operations. As this count could include civilians, we filtered out women as well as men outside the 18-65 age group. And if someone lived and died in the four Ukrainian regions occupied by Russia, we excluded them as a possible civilian â unless he had a record of military service attached to his entry. Another 14,093 entries were identified by looking at employment, and 51,067 were recorded in the database as deceased on the basis of a court ruling. This often happens when a soldier goes missing in a combat zone for more than six months and their body has not been recovered. Again, we filtered out civilians by only counting deaths in the war zones in Ukraine and Russia. According to BBC Russian's analysis of the leaked files, in the first year of the war the average age of those killed was 34. By 2025, as prisoners and contract soldiers entered the ranks, it had risen to 40 (38 according to our own list). Some of Russia's poorest regions in Eastern Siberia account for a disproportionately large share of the losses. Men from Tyva, Buryatia and Zabaykalsky Krai are 20-25 times more likely to die in the war than residents of the biggest cities of Moscow and St Petersburg. Image source, AFP via Getty Images In most regions, the distribution of deaths based on Rosstat data differs from that in the BBC's list by just a few tenths of a percentage point. At least 5,017 foreigners are among those who died fighting for Russia, according to our analysis of the Rosstat files, including 1,031 Uzbeks and 720 Tajiks. We have left out Ukrainians from this count to avoid including civilians. This is a conservative estimate as dual nationals are listed as Russians in the database, and there is no reference to North Koreans who died repelling the Ukrainian incursion into Russia in 2024. The BBC identified 2,304 North Korean soldiers who died there by analysing satellite imagery and official photographs of a newly built memorial in Pyongyang. The leaked Russian statistics may not be complete but taken in conjunction with BBC Russian's own work they are significant. In the context of a war that has lasted four years and 10 months, these are high numbers for Russia, when compared with the Soviet war in Afghanistan that ended in 1989. In that 10-year war, an estimated 15,000 Red Army troops died, and an estimated one million civilians were killed.
